explanations.explanation: Oh, friend, that one's a trap, and I walked right up to it too. Paul says the opposite: "It is no trouble for me to write the same things to you again…" (Philippians 3:1). He isn't groaning about a chore. He's glad to write it, and I think that says a lot about how much he cares for the Philippians.
You've got it, baker. Paul says, "It is no trouble for me to write the same things to you again…" (Philippians 3:1). Nobody's rolling their eyes at the pen here. He's happy to say it again.

Right on the money, baker. Paul says writing the same things again is "a safeguard for you" (Philippians 3:1). A safeguard keeps you protected, like an oven mitt for the soul. Hearing it twice is not a waste when it keeps you safe.

I see why that sounds right, friend. Repeating things can feel heavy, like carrying a full tray with no mitts. But Paul doesn't call it a burden. He says it "is a safeguard for you" (Philippians 3:1).

Nope, no scolding in this line, friend. Paul isn't pointing a finger and saying "I told you so." He says the same things again are "a safeguard for you" (Philippians 3:1). That's a protection, not a telling-off.
That's the one, baker. Paul says they are the ones "who glory in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 3:3). Their pride and their joy sit on Him, not on themselves. Nice and clear.

Moses was Israel's leader who received the law, so I get the guess, friend. But Paul never names Moses in this verse. He says they "glory in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 3:3). That's where all the glory goes.

Abraham is a big name, friend, and I see why he came to mind. But Paul doesn't say a word about Abraham in this verse. The ones who worship by the Spirit of God are the ones "who glory in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 3:3).

Whoa, hold up, friend, that's flipped. Paul says the "we" are the ones "who put no confidence in the flesh" (Philippians 3:3). Not great confidence, none. They worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus instead.

That's right, baker. Paul says they are the ones "who put no confidence in the flesh" (Philippians 3:3). Their trust sits somewhere else entirely. They worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus.

You got it, baker. Paul says, "If anyone else thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, I have more" (Philippians 3:4). He's about to lay out a résumé that would make anybody sit up straight. Hold onto your apron.

Oh, friend, Paul isn't being modest on this one. He says, "If anyone else thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, I have more" (Philippians 3:4). He's about to show you the receipts, and it's a long list.
Close, but Paul goes a step past even. He says, "If anyone else thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, I have more" (Philippians 3:4). Not a tie, he's ahead. And then he lists it all.
That's right, baker. Paul says, "as to righteousness in the law, faultless" (Philippians 3:6). That's the top of his list, and he puts it there on purpose. It makes what he says next hit even harder.

Plot twist, friend, Paul really does say it. His words are, "as to righteousness in the law, faultless" (Philippians 3:6). That's him at the top of the list, and it's what makes his next line so surprising.

Yes, baker, that's what he says. "But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ" (Philippians 3:7). Everything he used to stack up as a win, he now counts as loss. That's quite a turn.

Hang on, friend, Paul really does say it. His words are, "But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ" (Philippians 3:7). The things he once counted as wins, he now counts as loss, for Christ's sake.

You've got it, baker. Paul counts all things as loss compared to "the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). Nothing else comes close to that. Not even a fresh batch, and you know how I feel about those.

Good guess, friend, since Paul called himself faultless in the law a couple of verses back. But that's the very thing he counts as loss. What outshines it is "the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8).

That one's on Paul's list, friend, so it makes sense you picked it. But it's part of what he counts as loss (Philippians 3:5, 7). The thing that beats it all is "the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8).
Yes, baker, that's his word. "I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ" (Philippians 3:8). Not a small word, and Paul meant it. Compared to knowing Christ, it all goes in the bin.
That's backwards, friend. Paul doesn't hold onto this stuff like a prize. He says, "I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ" (Philippians 3:8). The real treasure is Christ.
Sounds believable, friend, but that's not his word. Paul doesn't say it weighs on him like a bill. He says, "I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ" (Philippians 3:8).
Right, baker. Paul says he does not want "my own righteousness from the law" (Philippians 3:9). He had a faultless record there, and he still lets it go. That's how much he values what Christ gives.

That's the one, baker. Paul wants the righteousness that is "through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God on the basis of faith" (Philippians 3:9). It comes from God, not from our own record. Nobody has to bake their way into it.

Elders are leaders in a community, friend, but this verse doesn't mention them. Paul sets his own righteousness from the law against the righteousness "through faith in Christ" (Philippians 3:9). That's what goes in the blanks.

I can see why the temple came to mind, friend, since it was the center of worship. But Paul doesn't say a word about it in this verse. He sets righteousness from the law against righteousness "through faith in Christ" (Philippians 3:9).
Hope is a good word, friend, and a lovely thing to have. But it isn't the word in this verse. Paul says the righteousness from God comes "through faith in Christ" (Philippians 3:9).

Friend, I wish it worked like picking only the sprinkles, but Paul says both. He writes, "I want to know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings…" (Philippians 3:10). He's not choosing one and skipping the other.

That's right, baker. Paul wants the power of Christ's resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings together. He writes, "I want to know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death" (Philippians 3:10).
Yes, baker. Paul says, "and so, somehow, to attain to the resurrection from the dead" (Philippians 3:11). That's where the whole passage lands. It's the goal he's reaching for.

I'd sign up for that one too, friend, but it's not what Paul writes. He's just talked about the fellowship of Christ's sufferings, so easy isn't the picture. He wants "to attain to the resurrection from the dead" (Philippians 3:11).
Rest sounds nice, friend, and I know a baker who could use some. But that's not what Paul says here. He wants "to attain to the resurrection from the dead" (Philippians 3:11).
